title: Women workers in Saudi Arabia: 68 recorded suicides in six years, and families who doubt the cause
excerpt: New figures from welfare board records and research show how many women domestic workers come home dead or abused, and how few cases are investigated.
content:
Bangladeshi women who go to Saudi Arabia as domestic workers too often come home dead or scarred, and their deaths are rarely investigated, according to an investigation published by The Daily Star on 9 November that draws on welfare board records and research.

The numbers

  • 2017 to 2022: 705 bodies of women migrant workers were repatriated. 110 deaths were recorded as suicide, 68 of them in Saudi Arabia. About 32% of all deaths were classed as unnatural (RMMRU study, 2023, using Wage Earners’ Welfare Board records).
  • Families’ doubts: of 100 bereaved families interviewed, 48 questioned the cause on the death certificate, and 11 asked for a second post-mortem but were told it was not possible.
  • 2023: 101 bodies returned, 20 recorded suicides, 13 from Saudi Arabia. 2025: 88 bodies, 14 recorded suicides, 13 from Saudi Arabia (Wage Earners’ Welfare Board documents).
  • Abuse: in a 2019 government study of 110 women who returned from Saudi Arabia, 35% reported physical and sexual abuse and 44% said they were not paid regularly.
  • Migration trend: women’s overseas employment fell from 105,466 in 2022 to 62,317 in 2025. Saudi Arabia took 44,832 of them in 2025, making it the largest destination (RMMRU).

Who said what

Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), called for independent forensic examinations in Bangladesh: “We proposed introducing a system at the airport to examine bodies for visible signs of injury.”

Md Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC’s Migration Programme said complaints were often not pursued with Saudi authorities. Nanjiba Kabir, a case management officer at BRAC’s Migration Welfare Centre, said nearly 90% of returning domestic workers she had met had faced physical or psychological abuse. BRAC has assisted about 350 women returnees this year.

The state minister for expatriates’ welfare told parliament on 3 September that the government has agreements with 22 law firms in 13 countries and runs two safe homes in Saudi Arabia. On 4 November, Deputy Speaker Kayser Kamal called for a review of the 2015 Bangladesh-Saudi agreement on women domestic workers.

Why it matters

Migration, women’s rights and legal aid organisations are often the only support for returnees and bereaved families. The figures make a strong evidence base for advocacy on independent post-mortems, pre-departure training, embassy case handling and a revised bilateral agreement.

What to watch

Whether the government reviews the 2015 agreement, introduces forensic checks for repatriated bodies, and publishes full annual data on deaths and abuse cases.
